text: Canada's first climate lawsuit to go to trial has wrapped up hearings. Many more are underway. Science # Canada's first climate lawsuit to go to trial has wrapped up hearings. Many more are underway ## Youth lawsuit in Federal Court paves way for other cases questioning governments' duty to ensure safe climate What level of responsibility does the federal government bear for the climate disasters Canadians are suffering? That's the question at the heart of a landmark lawsuit that wrapped up witness testimony in Federal Court in Vancouver on Friday, and whose outcome could have a big influence on how a growing number of other climate lawsuits in Canada pan out. *La Rose et al. v Canada*, brought by 15 youth applicants in 2019 who say the federal government's inadequate actions to reduce carbon emissions is violating their constitutional rights, was heard over the past five weeks — the first full trial for a climate lawsuit in Canada. A dozen expert witnesses testified, along with the young people themselves. Andrea Rodgers, deputy director at Our Children's Trust, a legal non-profit that's supporting the case, said it's been "an incredible journey" for the plaintiffs and she hopes the case will inspire "a body of law that will continue to evolve." "I think if there's one thing many people can agree on, it's that the interests of our children should be prioritized and protected. And this case gives the courts in Canada the opportunity to do that for Canadian youth," Rodgers said Friday. But even as the historic hearings took place, more cases of climate-related litigation appeared. On Nov. 18, a <u>lawsuit was filed</u> against the province of Quebec for delaying an emissions target. A <u>lawsuit</u> to force Canada's largest pension fund to better manage climate risk had an important <u>hearing</u> in November. Two other cases — <u>a youth lawsuit</u> seeking a more stringent climate plan in Ontario and a <u>Federal Court case</u> arguing the federal government is not following its own climate law — are also chugging along. ## **Lawsuits building off each other** Fraser Thomson, a lawyer at environmental law charity Ecojustice, said as the various cases have gone through the court system, they've "built off each other" by winning legal arguments to pave the way for following cases. "As more and more courts look at the indisputable evidence that shows that climate change poses an existential threat, courts are increasingly choosing to entertain these arguments and in some cases to weigh in favour of them on certain legal issues," Thomson said. Thomson is not involved in *La Rose*, but he is a lawyer for the plaintiffs in a newly filed federal lawsuit, *Maltais et al. v Canada*, as well as a long running Ontario case, *Mathur et al. v Ontario.* *Mathur* was filed in 2019 after Ontario Premier Doug Ford's government weakened the province's emissions targets. The plaintiffs argued that exposed them to climate harms and violated their constitutional rights to life, liberty and security, as well as equality. The case was initially dismissed by the first level of court, but then sent back for a full hearing by the appeal court. Right before *Mathur* was to receive a hearing in 2025 , the Ford government repealed the law requiring it to set an emissions target at all, and the case was put on hold. Thomson said he hopes to be back in front of a judge in early 2027 to get some clarity on the path forward. A rally outside the International Court of Justice in 2025 ahead of an advisory opinion on what legal obligations nations have to address climate change. (Peter Dejong/The Associated Press) Meanwhile, *Maltais* targets the government's own Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act. Thomson said "the law says the government has to have a plan" to set and meet its emissions targets, making it a more straightforward argument in court. It got an early boost this summer when the judge decided the case could proceed after the government asked for it to be dismissed. The two sides will now exchange written arguments, Thomson said. ## **Evolving climate science boosting cases** The government's defence in *La Rose* relied, in part, on the fact that Canada's emissions form a very small part of global emissions and therefore it alone cannot turn the tide on global warming. The government's witnesses helped bolster this argument this past week, speaking about the challenges of influencing the global climate, even though Canada is a major fossil fuel producer. Andrew Leach, an energy and environmental economist at the University of Alberta, testified that even if Canada stopped exporting millions of barrels of oil per day to the U.S., you couldn't assume "those emissions would not occur" because the U.S. could find that oil elsewhere and consume it anyway. But those emissions still have a measurable impact, and they have been made clearer through huge improvements in climate science. In recent years, researchers have been able to attribute specific climate disasters like heat waves and floods to climate change, and link emissions of specific fossil fuel producers to changes in the climate. "In many situations, people are producing scientific reports from the very governments that they are suing. And, so, it's very difficult to be a lawyer from the government and to challenge the findings of a scientific report prepared by your own client," Thomson said. The judges at the International Court of Justice as they delivered an advisory opinion on international climate obligations in 2025. (Peter Dejong/The Associated Press) Camille Martini, a doctoral researcher at Université Laval who studies global climate litigation, said lawsuits abroad have also helped drive the "wave" of cases being filed in Canada. Martini also pointed to the importance of a <u>legal opinion</u> released by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) last year, which said countries have a legal duty to address climate change under international law. Later, Canada co-sponsored a non-binding resolution in the UN's General Assembly supporting the ICJ's opinion. The resolution was adopted with a vast majority of countries in favour. "The ICJ opinion clarified … It's really binding on states to do the utmost possible based on each state's capabilities," Martini said, meaning countries can't say they don't have to act because their own emissions are too small. "So, I think now is the time for Canada to face the music." Lawyers for both sides in the *La Rose* case will return to court in February, where they will have a week to make their closing statements.
